newsitem.title: FRANCE: TENNIS-KAFELNIKOV SETS UP SEMIFINAL WITH QUALIFIER KORDA.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-KAFELNIKOV SETS UP SEMIFINAL WITH QUALIFIER KORDA.

text.p: Yevgeny Kafelnikov, the highest surviving seed in the Paris Open, beat Dutchman Paul Haarhuis in straight sets on Friday to set up a semifinal against Czech qualifier Petr Korda.
Kafelnikov won his quarter-final 7-6 6-1 after Korda, playing his ninth match of the Bercy tournament, eliminated French hope Arnaud Boetsch 7-6 7-6.
Haarhuis, who had beaten the Russian in their previous two meetings last year, saved three set points in the tie-break before losing it 9-7 and then faded in the second set.
Earlier, Magnus Gustafsson ensured there would be a Swedish finalist when he beat 1994 runner-up Marc Rosset of Switzerland 6-2 3-6 6-2 in the first quarter-final.
Gustafsson, who upset Andre Agassi in the second round, will meet one of his fellow Swedes Stefan Edberg, the 1990 winner, or 12th seed Thomas Enqvist, in the semifinals.
The last time only two seeds reached the quarter-finals was in 1988 -- American defending champion Tim Mayotte and Russia's Andrei Chesnokov.

Veteran Korda, coming back after nearly quitting tennis last year because of injury, said: "After the U.S. Open I locked myself inside the hall and just worked, you know, hitting balls, serving, hitting balls, serving, just like that every day.

"Suddenly I started to play well in Ostrava. Unfortunately, I couldn't play (in Stuttgart) last week because I didn't make time for qualifying because I was in the final in Ostrava," added Korda, who last had to qualify in Vienna in 1989.

Boetsch, who played brilliantly in eliminating second seed Michael Chang 6-1 6-3 in the third round on Thursday night, served for the first set at 6-5 but was broken, forcing a tie-break which Korda, ranked five places below Boetsch at 37, won 7-2.
At 5-5 in the second set tiebreak, Korda double faulted to give Boestch another chance to serve for a set. But the Czech saved the point with a fine passing shot.

Fortune favoured the more adventurous, less nervous Korda, and a net cord ball that dropped in the Frenchman's court gave him the chance to serve for the match, taking the tiebreak 8-6 when Boetsch netted a return.
"I felt a little heavier than yesterday," Boetsch said afterwards. "He played very well and gave me a lot of trouble with his left-handed serve."
"It's true he had the luck, but in the second set I led 3-1, 4-2 and served for the set. I should have sewn it up and not played with chance," Boetsch said.
Korda may have made more unforced errors, but he also had far more winning shots.

Gustafsson overcame a net cord controversy that upset him in the second set when the detector for serves sounded during a rally that he won. First the umpire, and then the referee, ordered the point to be replayed.
"In all the years I've been playing, if there was confusion over a point, play was stopped, but here it wasn't. I was upset when they said we had to replay the point," Gustafsson said.
"We both started to play worse tennis. It destroyed the rhythm of the match."
The detector sounded several times during the set before being turned off. It was adjusted for the third.

The 29-year-old Swede, who was out of the game for a year following shoulder surgery and may need another operation, had the measure of Rosset's booming service, the fastest recorded in the Bercy tournament at 207 kph.
"I like his serve, even if it's very hard. I have more trouble with some slower serves," said Gustafsson, whose returns often surprised the Swiss, who served 16 aces to only two from the Swede.

Gustafsson said he takes anti-inflammatory pills for his shoulder -- "it's not so bad as to need injections" -- and would have X-rays after next week's Stockholm tournament to determine whether he needed more surgery.
